title: Accident Compensation Corporation

{{Short description|New Zealand Crown entity}} {{Use New Zealand English|date=April 2024}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Infobox government agency | name = Accident Compensation Corporation | native_name = {{Native name|mi|Te Kaporeihana Āwhina Hunga Whara}} | type = [[Crown entity]] | logo = Accident Compensation Corporation logo.svg | jurisdiction = [[New Zealand Government]] | headquarters = [[Wellington]] | coordinates = {{coord|-41.274876|174.777701|type:landmark_region:NZ|display=inline}} | minister1_name = [[Scott Simpson (politician)|Scott Simpson]] | minister1_pfo = Minister for ACC | chief1_name = Megan Main | chief1_position = Chief Executive | website = {{URL|http://www.acc.co.nz/}} }} The '''Accident Compensation Corporation''' ('''ACC''') ({{langx|mi|Te Kaporeihana Āwhina Hunga Whara}}) is the New Zealand [[Crown entity]] responsible for administering the country's [[No-fault insurance|no-fault]] accidental injury compensation scheme, commonly referred to as the ACC scheme. The scheme provides financial compensation and support to citizens, residents, and temporary visitors who have suffered personal injuries. The corporation was founded as the '''Accident Compensation Commission''' on 1 April 1974 as a result of the Accident Compensation Act 1972. Its principal governing act today is the Accident Compensation Act 2001.{{cite web |url= http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2001/0049/latest/DLM99494.html |title= Accident Compensation Act 2001 -- New Zealand Legislation |publisher=Parliamentary Counsel Office}} As a Crown entity, ACC is governed by a board that is responsible to the Minister for ACC. Unlike most other Crown entities, it has its own dedicated ministerial portfolio, which since February 2025 has been held by [[Scott Simpson (politician)|Scott Simpson]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2023}} ==History== The ACC has its origins in the Workers' Compensation for Accidents Act 1900, which established a limited compensation scheme for workers who had suffered injuries where there was no directly responsible party. In 1966, a New Zealand [[Royal Commission]], chaired by High Court judge [[Owen Woodhouse]], was established. In 1967 the Royal Commission recommended extending this compensation to cover all injuries on a no-fault basis.{{cite web|url=https://nzhistory.govt.nz/page/accident-compensation-corporation-comes-existence|title=ACC comes into operation|date=1 April 1974|access-date=17 July 2020}} Following this report, the [[New Zealand Parliament]] passed the Accident Compensation Act 1972, later amended in 1973. The Accident Compensation Commission was established from 1 April 1974. In 1992, the commission was renamed the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC),{{cite web|url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/who-we-are/our-history/|title=ACC - Our history|date=17 July 2020}} as a short form for its official name ''Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Corporation''[ http://www.nzlii.org/nz/legis/hist_act/aracia19921992n13471.pdf ACC Act 1992] (part IX) The Act was later replaced by the Injury Prevention, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 2001, which was in 2010 renamed the Accident Compensation Act 2001. The Commission's annual report for 1989/90Annual Report (1989/90) of the Accident Compensation Commission, p.5 proposed that the distinction between accidents—which are coveredsee ''[[Fenton v. Thorley]]'' [1903] WN 149 for an old definition—and "illness"—which is not—should be dropped. This proposal was not taken up by the government. From 1 July 1999, the [[Fourth National Government of New Zealand|fourth National government]] allowed private insurance operators to provide work-related accident insurance, and ACC was briefly exposed to competition. The [[Fifth Labour Government of New Zealand|fifth Labour government]] (elected in November 1999) repealed this change, and as of 1 July 2000 re-instated ACC as the sole provider of accident insurance coverage. On 30 May 2025, ACC chair Tracey Batten resigned effective immediately. In March 2024, the [[Sixth National Government of New Zealand|sixth National Government]] had renewed a chairmanship for a further three-year term until 2027.{{cite news |title=ACC chair Tracey Batten resigns |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/562659/acc-chair-tracey-batten-resigns |access-date=30 May 2025 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=30 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250530042851/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/562659/acc-chair-tracey-batten-resigns |archive-date=30 May 2025 |url-status=live}} ==Features== ACC is the sole and compulsory provider of accident insurance in New Zealand for all work and non-work related injuries. The corporation administers the ACC Scheme on a no-fault basis, so that anyone, regardless of the way in which they suffered an injury, has coverage under the scheme. Due to the scheme's no-fault basis, people who have suffered personal injury do not have the right to sue an at-fault party, except for [[exemplary damages]].see, ''Donselaar v Donselaar'' [1982] 1 NZLR 97, confirmed by ''Auckland City Council v Blundell'' [1986] 1 NZLR 732. As of July 2026, the scheme does not cover injuries received by volunteer firefighters in their service in relation to mental injuries received due to trauma, to the same extent as their paid firefighters.{{Cite news |last=Palmer |first=Russell |date=2026-07-23 |title=Bill to extend ACC cover to volunteer firefighters drawn |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/775974/bill-to-extend-acc-cover-to-volunteer-firefighters-drawn |access-date=2026-07-24 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]]}}{{Cite news |date=2026-07-23 |title=Volunteer firefighters bill drawn from ballot in bid for equal ACC cover |url=https://newswire.co.nz/2026/07/volunteer-firefighters-acc-cover-bill-mcanulty-ballot/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |work=Newswire}} However, the Accident Compensation Act 2001 defines "personal injury" in a manner that restricts the concept of injury to physical injury or a mental injury due to a physical injury.{{Cite web |title=Accident Compensation Act 2001 section 26 |url=https://legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2001/0049/latest/DLM100910.html?search=sw_096be8ed81f1da19_%22personal+injury%22_25_se&p=1&sr=14}} Only mental injury caused by sexual assault has been excluded from the definition of personal injury and the claimant does not have to prove physical injury {{Cite web |title=Accident Compensation Act 2001, section 20 |url=https://legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2001/0049/latest/DLM100687.html?search=sw_096be8ed81f1da19_%22personal+injury%22_25_se&p=1}} The scheme provides a range of entitlements to injured people, however 93.5 percent of new claims in 2011 to 2012 were for treatment costs only. Other entitlements include weekly compensation for lost earnings (paid at a rate of 80% of a person's pre-injury earnings) and the cost of home or vehicle modifications for the seriously injured. The scheme offers entitlements subject to various eligibility criteria. ACC works with partners and communities on initiatives to prevent injuries. These initiatives include "RugbySmart" with [[New Zealand Rugby]],{{Cite web|url=http://www.sporty.co.nz/nzrf/Injury/Rugby-Smart|title=NZ Rugby Foundation - Rugby Smart|website=www.sporty.co.nz|access-date=2017-07-06}} "Ride Forever",{{Cite news|url=https://www.rideforever.co.nz/about/|title=About » Ride Forever|access-date=2017-07-06|language=en-US|archive-date=28 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828224305/http://www.rideforever.co.nz/about/|url-status=dead}} "Mates and Dates",{{Cite web|url=https://www.acc.co.nz/preventing-injury/sexual-violence/|title=Preventing sexual violence|website=www.acc.co.nz|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06}} and "Make Your Home a Safety Zone" with Safekids Aotearoa.{{Cite web|url=http://www.safekids.nz/Safety-Topics/Details/Type/View/ID/14715/Home-Safety|title=Make your home a safety zone|website=www.starship.org.nz/safekids|language=en-US|access-date=2017-07-06}} It is claimed that the system encourages clinicians to report mistakes. The cost of litigation to the health system is considerably less than in some other countries.{{cite book |last1=Hunt |first1=Jeremy |title=Zero |date=2022 |publisher=Swift Press |location=London |isbn=9781800751224 |page=127 }} == Alternative therapies == ACC has been criticised for providing funding for several [[Alternative medicine|alternative therapies]] that are unsupported by scientific evidence, including [[acupuncture]], [[osteopathy]] and [[chiropractic]] interventions.{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=Rachel |date=2016-04-29 |title=ACC paid out $163 million on alternative therapies and physiotherapy in 2015 |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/79403740/acc-paid-out-163-million-on-alternative-therapies-and-physiotherapy-in-2015 |access-date=2023-02-21 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}} ==Funding== ACC is primarily funded through a combination of levies and government contributions. Income collected from each source goes into predetermined accounts based on the source. Costs relating to an injury are paid from one of these accounts based on the type and cause of the injury. The four main accounts are: Work, Earners, Non-Earners, and Motor Vehicle. There is also a fifth account: Treatment Injury (formerly Medical Misadventure), that draws on both the Earners and Non-Earners accounts.{{Cite web |title=What your levies pay for |url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/our-levies/what-your-levies-pay |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=ACC |language=en}} Levy rates were most recently approved by [[Cabinet of New Zealand|Cabinet]] in November 2021 after a final recommendation from ACC Minister [[Carmel Sepuloni]], for the 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 levy periods. Levy periods run from the {{Date|1st of April|DMY}} to the {{Date|31st of March|DMY}} the following year.{{Cite web |title=Levy results |url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/our-levies/levy-results |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=ACC |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Paying levies if you own or drive a vehicle |url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/our-levies/paying-levies-if-you-own-or-drive-a-vehicle |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=ACC |language=en}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! width="12%" | Account !! width="25%" |Types of injury covered !! Income sources |- | Work || Work-related || Levies collected from employers and self-employed people. The amount payable averages 0.63% of an employer's payroll or income earned ({{Asof|2024|April|1|df=NZ|lc=y}}), though rates vary depending on the employer's industry and risks associated with it. |- | Earners || Non-work-related, by income-earners || Levies collected in conjunction with tax deductions on income. Paid by employees through PAYE or by self-employed people directly. The amount payable is 1.39% of income earned ({{Asof|2024|April|1|df=NZ|lc=y}}). |- | Non-earners || Non-work-related, by non-income-earners
(i.e. children, the elderly and unemployed, visitors) || Government contribution from the general taxation pool. |- | Motor Vehicle || Relating to motor vehicles on public roads || Levies included in the price of petrol (not diesel or LPG), and through motor vehicle license fees. The levy on motor vehicle license fees averages $113.94 ([[Goods and Services Tax (New Zealand)|GST]]-exclusive) per vehicle per year ({{Asof|2024|April|1|df=NZ|lc=y}}), with motorcycles and heavy vehicles paying more than average due to the increased likelihood of injury associated with these modes of transport, and the petrol levy is set at 6c per litre (GST-exclusive). |- | Treatment Injury || As a result of medical treatment (previously known as medical misadventure) || Funded from the Earners and Non-Earners accounts, depending on the clients' employment status. |}[[File:Accident Compensation Corporation Palmerston North.JPG|thumb|Palmerston North offices]]ACC initially had a "fully funded" model whereby sufficient levies were collected to cover the lifetime cost of each injury, which might require compensation over a period of 30 years or more. The scheme was shifted to a "pay-as-you-go" funding model, where the scheme collects enough levies during a year to cover the cost of claims for that particular year, in 1982.{{Cite web|url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/who-we-are/our-history/|title=Our history|website=ACC}} The “fully funded” model was restored in 1999. However, getting ACC onto a strong financial footing was not easy and in 2009, ACC posted a $4.8 billion loss—at the time described as the biggest corporate loss in New Zealand's history. This cost escalation is thought to have been due to an increase in the number of claims, a widening of entitlements and increased costs of meeting the claims.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/sunday-star-times/2952015/The-painful-bills-about-to-wallop-your-wallet|archive-url=https://archive.today/20110613104931/http://www.stuff.co.nz/sunday-star-times/news/2952015/The-painful-bills-about-to-wallop-your-wallet|url-status=dead|title=The painful bills about to wallop your wallet|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=2019-03-25|archive-date=2011-06-13}} Another factor was [[physiotherapy]] services being made free at the point of delivery leading to over-servicing of clients.{{Cite web|url=http://www.acc.co.nz/PRD_EXT_CSMP/idcplg?IdcService=GET_FILE&dID=10729&dDocName=PRD_CTRB110770&allowInterrupt=1|title=Physiotherapy claims summary|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160215144431/http://www.acc.co.nz/PRD_EXT_CSMP/idcplg?IdcService=GET_FILE&dID=10729&dDocName=PRD_CTRB110770&allowInterrupt=1|archive-date=2016-02-15|url-status=dead|access-date=2012-12-30}} Between 2000 and 2008 this appears to have contributed to an increase in physiotherapy costs of 214%.{{Cite web|url=http://www.acc.co.nz/news/PRD_CTRB113304|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216183143/http://www.acc.co.nz/news/PRD_CTRB113304|url-status=dead|title=ACC moves to curtail rise in physiotherapy costs|archive-date=February 16, 2013}} The 100% reimbursement scheme for physiotherapist services was ended, and ACC levies on wages and motorists were increased.{{cite news|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/2952114/The-painful-bills-about-to-wallop-your-wallet|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091011224920/http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/2952114/The-painful-bills-about-to-wallop-your-wallet|url-status=dead|archive-date=11 October 2009|title=The painful bills about to wallop your wallet|last=Armstrong|first=Grahame|date=11 October 2009|work=[[Sunday Star-Times]]|access-date=24 May 2011}} ACC chairman John Judge told the ''Sunday Star-Times'' that it was going to take a "hard-nosed" approach to get ACC into a sustainable position. This would require "substantial" levy increases and "legislative change to get people off the scheme and back to work quicker". By 2012, ACC had made good progress towards its 2019-goal (of being fully funded), and was $4.5 billion short of matching liabilities ($28.5b) with its assets ($24b).{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/politics/7143131/Funding-issue-brews-in-ACCs-cauldron|title=Funding issue brews in ACC's cauldron|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=20 June 2012 }} Towards the end of 2012, ACC Minister [[Judith Collins]] announced that Government would not cut ACC levies for the 2013–14 year. While the ACC Board and Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment had recommended reducing the levies by between 12 and 17 per cent, Collins stated that the government's decision was motivated by the uncertain economic conditions and a desire to ensure that reductions to the levy were sustainable. [[Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)|Andrew Little]], the Labour Party's ACC spokesman, criticised this decision, claiming that it was driven by the government's attempt to bring the budget into surplus and reducing the levy would provide a boost to the economy.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10859851|title=Govt ignored ministry call to trim ACC levies by $477m|date=January 17, 2013|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} In the 2013 budget, Collins announced a $1.3 billion cut in ACC levies over the next two years. Collins said the Earners and Workers accounts were now fully funded after the Corporation reduced the number of long term ACC claimants from 14,000 to less than 11,000.[http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10886118 ACC leads good economic news at National party convention] NZ Herald 25 May 2013 In 2015/16, ACC's outstanding claims liability (OCL) increased by $6.4 billion, which lead to a net deficit of $3.4 billion. The OCL measures the future cost of all existing ACC claims. That year also saw 1.93 million claims accepted; a 5.2% increase from the previous year. $3.5 billion was paid out to all new and existing claims.{{Cite web|url=https://www.acc.co.nz/about-us/media-releases/latest-news/acc-strong-financial-position/|title=ACC's outstanding claims liability|website=www.acc.co.nz|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06}}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} There has been some conjecture over whether or not ACC staff were paid incentives to remove long term clients off weekly compensation. This was refuted by Ex-CEO Ralph Stewart in 2012. That year there were 10,400 long-term claimants registered with ACC—down by over 1,000.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/politics/7158296/Ex-boss-defends-ACC-rehabilitation-policy|title=Ex-boss defends ACC rehabilitation policy|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=24 June 2012 }} In 2019, ACC posted a record $8.7 billion loss. ===Investments=== [[File:ACC building Otepoti.jpg|thumb|The ACC Ōtepoti building in Dunedin opened in August 2025, and is a four-storey building with a facade resembling a pou (flax basket).{{Cite news |last=Lewis |first=John |date=20 Aug 2025 |title=Dunedin ACC building ready for staff |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/dunedin-acc-building-ready-staff |access-date=28 Feb 2026 |work=[[Otago Daily Times]]}}]] ACC invests the premium it collects in various ventures. It has a portfolio of $40b and its investment manager was believed to be the highest paid public servant in New Zealand.{{cite news |title=ACC employee's pay tops $800,000 |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/acc-employees-pay-tops-800000/LVVQT4KVFLEDML4O7BI33Z4M34/ |access-date=1 February 2022 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=23 October 2014}} Of its top 50 investments, 47 are listed companies in NZ and overseas. Notable exceptions include a 22% shareholding in [[Kiwibank]] and the consortiums building [[Transmission Gully Motorway]] and the [[Auckland Northern Motorway#Under construction|Puhoi to Wellsford Motorway]].{{cite web |url=https://www.acc.co.nz/assets/corporate-documents/a62a168a11/acc7811-annual-report-2017.pdf|title=Annual report 2017|website=acc.co.nz|access-date=9 April 2023}} ACC has attracted controversy at several junctures since its establishment due to the nature of some its investment decisions. In 2003 Green Party MP [[Sue Bradford]] revealed that ACC held investments in brewery industry giants DB Breweries and Lion Nathan, which she claimed contravened ACC's legal obligation to engage in ethical investments to protect New Zealand's global reputation.{{Cite web |date=May 13, 2003 |title=ACC booze investments 'unethical' |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0305/S00303.htm |access-date=2023-06-21 |website=www.scoop.co.nz}} In 2016 ACC admitted it had indirectly invested in six companies on its own exclusion list, including weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin and British Tobacco.{{Cite web |date=2016-08-29 |title=ACC invested in banned companies |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/311999/acc-invested-in-banned-companies |access-date=2023-06-22 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}} ACC's ethical investment policy was drawn into question again in 2019, when Green Party MP Chlöe Swarbrick publicly criticised the Crown Entity for continued investment in fossil fuels, arguing that in light of the climate emergency this investment was unethical and that divestment should take place according to the precedent set by its exclusion of investment in tobacco companies.{{Cite web |last=Coughlan |first=Thomas |date=2019-08-08 |title=ACC questioned over billion-dollar fossil fuel investments |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/114842000/acc-questioned-over-billiondollar-fossil-fuel-investments |access-date=2023-06-22 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}} ===Cover for the self-employed=== ACC CoverPlus Extra was introduced by ACC to provide cover for self-employed workers and business owners that would fail to otherwise be covered adequately by the standard ACC CoverPlus policy. It works by paying an agreed level of compensation, in the event of an injury resulting in time off from work.{{Cite web|url=https://www.acc.co.nz/for-business/choosing-the-best-cover-option/types-of-cover-for-self-employed/|title=Types of cover for self-employed|website=www.acc.co.nz|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06}} With this cover already agreed upon, any business would not have to prove loss of income and has certainty on their amount of cover in the event of an accident-related injury. The ACC CoverPlus policy was designed to cover employees at 80% of their net taxable income. With ACC CoverPlus Extra, a self-employed contractor would get 100% of the pre-agreed compensation paid until they were fit to return to full-time work. A business owner would be able to get compensation under ACC CoverPlus Extra even if the business continued to earn income whilst the business owner could not work because of injury. This would not be possible with the standard policy. ===Accredited Employers' Programme=== ACC allows certain companies to manage and fund the claims of its employees who are injured at work. In return, they are given a large discount in ACC premium. ACC says this provides companies with a financial incentive to have good health and safety practices at work.{{cite web |title=Joining the Accredited Employers Programme (AEP) |url=https://www.acc.co.nz/for-business/understanding-your-cover-options/accredited-employers-programme/ |website=ACC |access-date=8 July 2022}} More than 140 New Zealand employers participate in this programme. ACC Futures Coalition and Green Party criticize this programme because creates a conflict interest for employers to wrongly deny claims and say it should be cancelled.{{cite news |last1=Mead |first1=Thomas |title=Exclusive: Minister admits ACC's Accredited Employer Programme has 'flaws' |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2021/11/24/exclusive-minister-admits-accs-accredited-employer-programme-has-flaws/ |access-date=8 July 2022 |work=[[1News]] |date=24 November 2021}} ==Notable events== ===Violence against staff === ACC clients have occasionally threatened or attempted to harm ACC staff. In 1999, a staff member was fatally stabbed by a claimant at an ACC office in [[Henderson, New Zealand|Henderson]].{{Cite news |date=2000-08-16 |title=ACC murder spurs security beef-up |language=en-NZ |newspaper=[[New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/acc-murder-spurs-security-beef-up/7FACLSB4V6UCO5LCEPWCCNML6M |access-date=2023-07-19 |issn=1170-0777}} In 2010, ACC logos were removed from company vehicles after several staff had their cars rammed or were "driven off the road by other drivers". The following year a threat against former chief executive Ralph Stewart led to a decision for security staff to be posted outside his home. There have been at least two threats to blow up a [[car bomb]] outside ACC offices and police have had to be called on several other occasions. In 2012, there were a total of 134 recorded threats made against staff—the majority against case managers "making difficult decisions".{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/8465429/ACC-staff-in-line-of-fire|title=ACC staff in line of fire|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=23 March 2013 }} ===Client fraud=== In 2013, it was reported that 64 people have been convicted of defrauding ACC of a total of more than $10 million over the past four years. This includes clients claiming they were "injured" but who kept working while receiving ACC benefits and medical practitioners who billed ACC for more treatment than they actually provided. Another category of ACC fraudster includes widows who continued claiming payments after their (injured) partners have subsequently died. Sometimes these payments went on for nearly 30 years before the fraud came to light, with one woman having received nearly $150,000 after her husband had died.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10859641|title=ACC frauds hit $10m over past four years|first=Jared |last=Savage Investigative reporter, NZ Herald|date=January 16, 2013|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} ===Staff fraud=== ACC staff have defrauded the corporation on a number of occasions. Jeffrey Chapman, former ACC chief executive from 1985 to 1992, was imprisoned for defrauding ACC and other government agencies; Gavin Robins, his successor from 1993 to 1997, was also charged with fraud but was acquitted.Don Rennie, [https://www.victoria.ac.nz/law/research/publications/vuwlr/prev-issues/pdf/vol-34-2003/issue-2/rennie.pdf "Administering Accident Compensation in the 1980s", (2003)] 34 VUWLR 329, 348 In 2011, a senior manager was convicted of dishonesty offences involving property leased to ACC by private business interests.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/news/article.cfm?c_id=3&objectid=10712556|title=Former ACC property boss escapes jail over bribe|date=14 March 2011|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} In late 2012, Jonathan Wright, an ACC-contracted medical assessor, was convicted of dishonestly obtaining over $18,000 in falsified travel expenses from ACC.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10851190|title=ACC fraud doctor named in court|first=Kurt |last=Bayer |date=30 November 2012|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} ===Treatment-injury claims=== A treatment injury is one caused in the course of treatment by a registered health professional, and are not a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.{{Cite news|url=http://communitylaw.org.nz/community-law-manual/chapter-19-accident-compensation/injuries-and-conditions-covered-by-acc-chapter-19/|title=Injuries and conditions covered by ACC - Community Law|work=Community Law|access-date=2017-07-06|language=en-US}} Until 2005, these were called "medical misadventure" claims. Treatment injury covers harm during a procedure, misdiagnosis, failure in care such as delay in treatment. It is the treatment provider that lodges the claim with ACC. The Accident Compensation Corporation will then investigate the claim and either accept or decline the claim. ===Bronwyn Pullar privacy breach=== ACC has had a number of breaches of privacy relating to claimants. The most significant occurred in 2011 after the release of details of 6700 claimants to an ACC claimant, Bronwyn Pullar. Pullar had been battling ACC since suffering a head injury in 2002—and had 45 separate complaints against the agency—only one of which was about the privacy breaches.[http://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/politics/6631240/Full-list-of-Bronwyn-Pullars-complaints-against-ACC Full list of Bronwyn Pullar's complaints against ACC], [[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]] In 2011 she and former National Party president [[Michelle Boag]], had a meeting with two senior ACC managers to discuss her concerns. ACC referred the matter to the police claiming Pullar had threatened to go to the media about the privacy breaches if she didn't get what she wanted. The police listened to a tape recording of the meeting and decided there was no case to answer.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/comment/editorials/7054022/Editorial-Time-for-answers-ACC|title=Editorial: Time for answers, ACC|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=6 June 2012 }} In March 2012, ACC Minister [[Nick Smith (New Zealand politician)|Nick Smith]] resigned from Cabinet after it was revealed that he had written letters on behalf of Pullar, who was a personal friend of his, while he was ACC Minister.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10793534|title=Nick Smith bows out as minister|date=March 21, 2012|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} ACC chairman John Judge continued to insist his version of events was correct and as a result ACC Minister Judith Collins did not renew his tenure on the ACC Board. The chief executive of ACC, Ralph Stewart, also resigned the next day.[http://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/politics/7091963/ACC-boss-resigns-amid-political-pressure ACC boss resigns amid political pressure] ''[[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]]'' 13 June 2012 Three other board members—Murray Hilder, Rob Campbell, and John McCliskie—also resigned.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10814160|title=Murray Hilder resigns from ACC board|date=June 19, 2012|via=www.nzherald.co.nz}} The fallout from the affair continued in May 2012, when Collins sued Labour MPs [[Trevor Mallard]] and Andrew Little for defamation over comments they made on [[Radio New Zealand]] broadcasts linking her to the leak of an email from Michelle Boag following the release of the files.{{cite news| url= http://www.3news.co.nz/Mallard-served-papers-by-faux-constituent/tabid/1607/articleID/255817/Default.aspx| title= Mallard served papers by faux-constituent| date= 28 May 2012| access-date= 30 December 2012| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140419013857/http://www.3news.co.nz/Mallard-served-papers-by-faux-constituent/tabid/1607/articleID/255817/Default.aspx| archive-date= 19 April 2014| url-status= dead| df= dmy-all}} The case was settled after a High Court hearing in November 2012.[http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10847321 Judith Collins defamation case settled], [[The New Zealand Herald]], 14 November 2012 An independent review of ACC was conducted toward the end of 2012; it found the organisation "lacked a comprehensive strategy for protecting and managing claimants' information" and said ACC had an "almost cavalier" attitude toward its clients. The review showed that the culture within ACC enabled its staff to target clients involved in privacy breaches and complaints rather than demonstrating respect for claimants. In 2013, a "training academy" for staff was mooted, with an "emphasis on a client-centred approach".{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/editors-picks/8165257/Charm-school-for-ACC-staff|title=Charm school for ACC staff|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=10 January 2013 }} ==List of ministers== The following [[ministers in the New Zealand Government|ministers]] have held responsibility for the Accident Compensation Corporation.{{cite book |last= Wood |first= G.
